docs.title: Json Config
docs.text:
Layered JSON configuration with typed values. Describe your settings as a pydantic model, stack any number of JSON files on top of each other (defaults → workspace → user, ...) and read the merged result as a typed object. Edits are written back to a single layer, and only the values that differ from the layers below it are saved.

config = AppConfig(layer_filter="user")
config.resolve()                 # load the files and merge the layers
config.values.theme = "dark"
config.save()                    # user.json -> {"theme": "dark"}

def load(self) -> None:
    """Load values from *file_path* (if it exists)."""
    if self.file_path is None:
        return

    if not self.file_path.is_file():
        LOGGER.warning(
            f"[{self.name}] No file found at {self.file_path}, skipping load."
        )
        return
    text = self.file_path.read_text().strip()
    if not text:
        LOGGER.warning(
            f"[{self.name}] Empty file at {self.file_path}, skipping load."
        )
        return
    raw = json.loads(self.file_path.read_text())

    if not isinstance(raw, dict):
        raise ValueError(f"[{self.name}] Expected a JSON object in {self.file_path}")
    self._data = raw
    LOGGER.info(f"[{self.name}] Loaded from {self.file_path}")

def save(self) -> None:
    """Persist this layer's own values to *file_path*."""
    if self.file_path is None:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Layer '{self.name}' has no file_path set.")

    # If layer has no data and the file does not exist, skip saving.
    if not self.get_data() and not self.file_path.is_file():
        LOGGER.debug(f"[{self.name}] No data to save, skipping.")
        return

    self.file_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    with self.file_path.open("w") as fh:
        json.dump(self._data, fh, indent=4)
    LOGGER.info(f"[{self.name}] Saved to {self.file_path}")

docs.title: ConfigLayerManager(name)
docs.text:
Central manager that owns and resolves all config layers.

Usage::

manager = ConfigLayerManager("example")

# Register layers (order of registration does NOT matter;
# depends_on drives the merge order).
manager.register(ConfigLayer("main", file_path=Path("config/main.json")))
manager.register(ConfigLayer("user", depends_on=["main"],
    file_path=Path("config/user.json")))
manager.register(ConfigLayer("local", depends_on=["user"],
    file_path=Path("config/local.json")))

# Load all layers from disk.
manager.load_all()

# Get the fully-merged view.
cfg = manager.resolve()          # -> dict[str, Any]
cfg = manager.resolve("user")    # -> only main + user merged

# Modify a layer at runtime.
manager["user"].set(theme="dark")
manager.save("user")
```

#   root        (no parent)
#   child       (depends_on=["root"])

def register_from_paths_tree(
    self,
    tree: dict,
) -> None:
    """Build and register config layers from a nested directory path tree.

    The tree structure encodes parent-child dependencies directly.
    Each key is a directory path string; its value is either a nested
    dict of children, or an empty dict / set leaf.

    Args:
        tree (dict): Nested mapping of directory path strings.

    Example:
        ```python
        manager.register_from_paths({
            "configs/root.json": {
                "configs/root/child.json": {
                    "configs/root/child/grandchild.json": {}
                },
                "configs/root/other": {}
            }
        })
        # Registers:
        #   root        (no parent)
        #   child       (depends_on=["root"])
        #   grandchild  (depends_on=["child"])
        #   other       (depends_on=["root"])
        ```
    """

    def _walk(subtree: dict | set, parent_name: str | None) -> None:
        """Recursively walk the tree and register layers.

        Args:
            subtree (dict | set): The current subtree to walk.
            parent_name (str | None): The name of the parent layer, or None.
        """
        items = subtree if isinstance(subtree, dict) else {p: {} for p in subtree}
        for path_str, children in items.items():
            path = pathlib.Path(path_str)
            name = path.stem
            depends_on = [parent_name] if parent_name else []
            layer = ConfigLayer(
                name=name,
                depends_on=depends_on,
                file_path=path,
            )
            self.register(layer)
            LOGGER.debug(f"Registered layer '{name}' (depends_on={depends_on})")
            if children:
                _walk(children, name)

    _walk(tree, parent_name=None)

def resolve_many(self, *names: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Resolve multiple independent branches and merge them in order.

    Each name is resolved against its own subgraph (i.e. including its
    transitive dependencies), then the results are deep-merged left to
    right — so later names take precedence over earlier ones on conflicts.

    Args:
        names (*str): Layer names to resolve, in ascending priority order.

    Returns:
        dict[str, Any]: The merged config dictionary.

    Example:
        ```python
        # root → layer1
        # rooot → layer2
        cfg = manager.resolve_many("layer1", "layer2")
        # layer2 wins over layer1 on conflicting keys;
        # both override root.
        ```
    """
    return functools.reduce(
        layer_helpers.deep_merge_dicts,
        (self.resolve(name) for name in names),
        {},
    )

def seed_root_layers(self, defaults: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
    """Seed root layers with defaults and persist if file is absent.

    Args:
        defaults (dict[str, Any]): Dictionary of field names to default values
            to seed into root layers.
    """
    for name in self.sorted_names():
        layer = self[name]
        if layer.depends_on:
            continue

        missing = {k: v for k, v in defaults.items() if k not in layer._data}
        if missing:
            layer.set(**missing)
        if layer.file_path and not layer.file_path.is_file():
            layer.save()
            LOGGER.info(f"Initialized default config: '{layer.file_path}'")

docs.title: ConfigValues
docs.text:
Bases: BaseModel

Base class for config values.

Should be subclassed to define specific config fields.

A field may be given Field(alias="some_name") to mark it as a nested ConfigValues that should be represented as a nested object (keyed by its alias) rather than a plain attribute. This lets several logically-distinct sub-configs be combined into a single ConfigValues while still being addressable and resolvable as their own nested structures.

Example 
class MainWindowValues(ConfigValues):
    width: int = 100
    height: int = 100

class EnvValues(ConfigValues):
    name: str = "test"

class MainValues(ConfigValues):
    main_window: MainWindowValues = Field(
        default_factory=MainWindowValues, alias="main_window"
    )
    env: EnvValues = Field(default_factory=EnvValues, alias="env")
    root_value: int = 10

MainValues().to_dict()

# {
#     "main_window": {"width": 100, "height": 100},
#     "env": {"name": "test"},
#     "root_value": 10,
# }

@classmethod
def get_defaults(cls) -> dict[str, typing.Any]:
    """Return a dict of field/category names to their default values.

    Fields whose default value is itself a `ConfigValues` (typically
    given an alias) are expanded recursively into nested dicts, keyed by
    their alias (or their own attribute name if no alias is set).

    Returns:
        dict[str, Any]: dictionary of keys to their default values
    """
    defaults = {}
    for name, field in cls.model_fields.items():
        if field.default_factory is not None:
            value = field.default_factory()
        elif field.default is not None:
            value = field.default
        else:
            continue

        if isinstance(value, ConfigValues):
            value = value.get_defaults()

        defaults[cls._field_key(name, field)] = value

    return defaults

@classmethod
def get_field_bounds(
    cls, name: str
) -> tuple[int | float | None, int | float | None]:
    """Get the numeric bounds declared for a field.

    Reads the `ge`/`gt` and `le`/`lt` constraints given via
    `Field(...)` or `Annotated[...]`. Exclusive bounds (`gt`/`lt`) are
    returned as their raw constraint value.

    Args:
        name: The field's attribute name.

    Returns:
        tuple: `(minimum, maximum)`; a side is `None` if unbounded.

    Raises:
        KeyError: If no field called *name* exists.
    """
    field = cls.model_fields[name]
    minimum = maximum = None
    for constraint in field.metadata:
        for attr in ("ge", "gt"):
            if getattr(constraint, attr, None) is not None:
                minimum = getattr(constraint, attr)
        for attr in ("le", "lt"):
            if getattr(constraint, attr, None) is not None:
                maximum = getattr(constraint, attr)
    return minimum, maximum

def replace(self, data: dict[str, typing.Any]) -> typing.Self:
    """Update config values from a (possibly nested) dictionary.

    Keys are matched against each field's alias (if set) or its
    attribute name otherwise. Nested `ConfigValues` fields are updated
    recursively, so nested values absent from *data* are left untouched.

    *data* is passed through `pre_deserialize()` first, and the updated
    instance through `post_deserialize()` before being returned.

    Args:
        data (dict[str, Any]): dictionary of values to update

    Returns:
        ConfigValues: a new instance with updated values
    """
    data = self.pre_deserialize(data)
    updates: dict[str, typing.Any] = {}
    for name, field in type(self).model_fields.items():
        key = self._field_key(name, field)
        if key not in data:
            continue

        value = data[key]
        current = getattr(self, name)
        if isinstance(current, ConfigValues) and isinstance(value, dict):
            value = current.replace(value)
        updates[name] = value

    return self.model_copy(update=updates).post_deserialize()

@classmethod
def get_field_bounds(
    cls, name: str
) -> tuple[int | float | None, int | float | None]:
    """Get the numeric bounds declared for a field.

    Reads the `ge`/`gt` and `le`/`lt` constraints given via
    `Field(...)` or `Annotated[...]`. Exclusive bounds (`gt`/`lt`) are
    returned as their raw constraint value.

    Args:
        name: The field's attribute name.

    Returns:
        tuple: `(minimum, maximum)`; a side is `None` if unbounded.

    Raises:
        KeyError: If no field called *name* exists.
    """
    field = cls.model_fields[name]
    minimum = maximum = None
    for constraint in field.metadata:
        for attr in ("ge", "gt"):
            if getattr(constraint, attr, None) is not None:
                minimum = getattr(constraint, attr)
        for attr in ("le", "lt"):
            if getattr(constraint, attr, None) is not None:
                maximum = getattr(constraint, attr)
    return minimum, maximum

def replace(self, data: dict[str, typing.Any]) -> typing.Self:
    """Update config values from a (possibly nested) dictionary.

    Keys are matched against each field's alias (if set) or its
    attribute name otherwise. Nested `ConfigValues` fields are updated
    recursively, so nested values absent from *data* are left untouched.

    *data* is passed through `pre_deserialize()` first, and the updated
    instance through `post_deserialize()` before being returned.

    Args:
        data (dict[str, Any]): dictionary of values to update

    Returns:
        ConfigValues: a new instance with updated values
    """
    data = self.pre_deserialize(data)
    updates: dict[str, typing.Any] = {}
    for name, field in type(self).model_fields.items():
        key = self._field_key(name, field)
        if key not in data:
            continue

        value = data[key]
        current = getattr(self, name)
        if isinstance(current, ConfigValues) and isinstance(value, dict):
            value = current.replace(value)
        updates[name] = value

    return self.model_copy(update=updates).post_deserialize()

def register_from_paths_tree(
    self,
    tree: dict,
) -> None:
    """Build and register config layers from a nested directory path tree.

    The tree structure encodes parent-child dependencies directly.
    Each key is a directory path string; its value is either a nested
    dict of children, or an empty dict / set leaf.

    Args:
        tree (dict): Nested mapping of directory path strings.

    Example:
        ```python
        manager.register_from_paths({
            "configs/root.json": {
                "configs/root/child.json": {
                    "configs/root/child/grandchild.json": {}
                },
                "configs/root/other": {}
            }
        })
        # Registers:
        #   root        (no parent)
        #   child       (depends_on=["root"])
        #   grandchild  (depends_on=["child"])
        #   other       (depends_on=["root"])
        ```
    """

    def _walk(subtree: dict | set, parent_name: str | None) -> None:
        """Recursively walk the tree and register layers.

        Args:
            subtree (dict | set): The current subtree to walk.
            parent_name (str | None): The name of the parent layer, or None.
        """
        items = subtree if isinstance(subtree, dict) else {p: {} for p in subtree}
        for path_str, children in items.items():
            path = pathlib.Path(path_str)
            name = path.stem
            depends_on = [parent_name] if parent_name else []
            layer = ConfigLayer(
                name=name,
                depends_on=depends_on,
                file_path=path,
            )
            self.register(layer)
            LOGGER.debug(f"Registered layer '{name}' (depends_on={depends_on})")
            if children:
                _walk(children, name)

    _walk(tree, parent_name=None)

def deep_diff_dicts(current: dict, baseline: dict) -> dict:
    """Recursively compute the subset of *current* that differs from *baseline*.

    For keys present in both dicts as nested dicts, the diff is computed
    recursively so that only the genuinely-diverging leaf values are kept,
    dropping nested keys/sub-keys that match the baseline. All other
    (non-dict, or newly-added) values are kept as-is if they differ from
    (or are absent from) *baseline*.

    This is used to prune a config layer down to only its real overrides,
    including within nested category values.

    Args:
        current (dict): The full, resolved values to diff.
        baseline (dict): The values that would already be inherited without
            *current*'s own contribution.

    Returns:
        dict: A (possibly nested) dict containing only the differing values.
    """
    result = {}
    for key, value in current.items():
        base_value = baseline.get(key, UNSET_DICT_VALUE)
        if isinstance(value, dict) and isinstance(base_value, dict):
            nested_diff = deep_diff_dicts(value, base_value)
            if nested_diff:
                result[key] = nested_diff
        elif base_value is UNSET_DICT_VALUE or base_value != value:
            result[key] = value
    return result

    """Recursively merge *override* into *base*, returning a new dict.

def nest_value(path: Sequence[str], value: typing.Any) -> dict:
    """Wrap *value* in nested dicts following *path*.

    Example:
        ```python
        nest_value(("category_a", "field_one"), 42)
        # -> {"category_a": {"field_one": 42}}

    Args:
        path (Sequence[str]): Sequence of keys to nest the value under.
        value (typing.Any): The value to wrap.

    Returns:
        dict: The nested dict wrapping *value*.
    """
    result = value
    for key in reversed(path):
        result = {key: result}
    return result

def pop_nested(data: dict, path: Sequence[str]) -> None:
    """Remove the (possibly nested) value at *path* from *data*, in place.

    Any parent dict that becomes empty as a result of the removal is
    itself removed, so this never leaves behind stale, empty containers.

    Args:
        data (dict): The dict to remove the value from.
        path (Sequence[str]): Sequence of keys addressing the value to remove.
    """
    if not path:
        return

    key, *rest = path
    if key not in data:
        return

    if not rest:
        del data[key]
        return

    nested = data[key]
    if isinstance(nested, dict):
        pop_nested(nested, rest)
        if not nested:
            del data[key]

def topological_sort_layers(layers: dict[str, ConfigLayer]) -> list[str]:
    """Return layer names in dependency-resolved order (dependencies first).

    Uses `graphlib.TopologicalSorter` from the standard library.

    Args:
        layers (dict[str, ConfigLayer]): The layers to sort.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if a dependency is missing or not registered.
        graphlib.CycleError: if a circular dependency is detected.

    Returns:
        list[str]: The sorted layer names.
    """
    for name, layer in layers.items():
        for dep in layer.depends_on:
            if dep not in layers:
                raise ValueError(
                    f"Layer '{name}' depends on '{dep}', which is not registered."
                )

    graph = {name: set(layer.depends_on) for name, layer in layers.items()}
    return list(TopologicalSorter(graph).static_order())

docs.title: Developer Guide
docs.text: This guide is for people who work on json-config itself.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
uv sync
make check        # ruff + pytest
make mkdocs       # serve these docs

make help lists every target. Ruff uses a line length of 89 and the E, F and UP rules. Docstrings are Google style, because the API reference is generated from them (mkdocs-autoapi + mkdocstrings), so every public class and method needs one.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text: Page What you learn Architecture The modules, who calls whom, and the design decisions behind them. Resolution and saving How layers are ordered and merged, and how save() and revert_value() decide what to write. Testing Fixtures, the singleton reset, and what to cover. Releasing Branches, versions, the changelog and make release. API reference Generated from the docstrings (see the navigation).

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
json_config
├── api/            the public API: re-exports only
├── core/
│   ├── config_values.py   ConfigValues: pydantic model, to_dict / replace, hooks
│   ├── config_layer.py    ConfigLayer: one named layer of raw data, loads/saves a file
│   ├── layer_manager.py   ConfigLayerManager: owns layers, orders, merges, persists
│   └── config.py          LayeredConfig: typed values bound to a manager
├── utils/
│   └── layer_helpers.py   pure dict functions: merge, diff, nested get/pop, topo sort
└── version.py

Anything users should import goes through json_config/api/__init__.py and its __all__. Add new public names there.

docs.title: Data flow
docs.text:
JSON files ──load──▶ ConfigLayer._data ──merge (manager.resolve)──▶ dict
                                                                       │ ConfigValues.replace
                                                                       ▼
  JSON files ◀─save─── ConfigLayer._data ◀─diff (write_to_layer)─── ConfigValues (typed)
                                                                       ▲ to_dict

Layers hold plain dicts, never typed values. Typing happens only at the edge, in LayeredConfig: resolve() merges raw dicts and calls values.replace(...); save() calls values.to_dict(), diffs it against the layers below and stores the result on the layer. This keeps layers usable without a ConfigValues class (the manager can be driven directly) and means unknown keys in a file survive a load.

docs.title: ConfigValues
docs.text:
A pydantic BaseModel with populate_by_name and validate_assignment.

  • Aliases are the JSON keys. _field_key returns the alias if there is one and the attribute name otherwise. to_dict, replace, get_defaults and revert_value all go through it.
  • A nested ConfigValues field must have an alias. __pydantic_init_subclass__ enforces it (the plain __init_subclass__ runs before model_fields is filled in).
  • replace returns a new instance (model_copy(update=...)). It recurses into nested categories, so keys absent from the data keep their value. LayeredConfig reassigns self._values, which means a reference to the old values object goes stale after resolve().
  • Hooks (pre_/post_serialize, pre_/post_deserialize) are no-ops in the base class. Extension points are added as overridable hooks, not as extra constructor arguments or flags.

docs.title: ConfigLayer
docs.text:
A dataclass: name, depends_on, file_path, and _data.

  • load() skips a missing or empty file with a warning and raises ValueError for a non-object. It reads the file text twice (once to test for empty), which is harmless but is the first thing to fix if load performance matters.
  • save() creates parent directories, and does nothing when the layer has neither data nor a file, so empty layers don't litter the disk.
  • set, unset, unset_path, replace_data and get_data are the only supported ways to touch _data. get_data() returns a shallow copy.

docs.title: ConfigLayerManager
docs.text:
Owns name -> ConfigLayer. It is a named singleton: _ManagerMeta.__call__ caches one instance per name, and the constructor arguments of later calls are ignored. get_layer_manager(name) is the same as ConfigLayerManager(name). ConfigLayerManager.clear() empties the cache; it exists for tests.

It does not know about ConfigValues. seed_root_layers(defaults) takes a plain dict for that reason.

docs.title: LayeredConfig
docs.text: A generic class (PEP 695 syntax, hence Python 3.12+) with two required class attributes, VALUES_CLASS and NAME. __init__ raises NotImplementedError without NAME and instantiates VALUES_CLASS() for the initial values. It holds a layer_filter instead of a layer: the active layer is looked up by name each time, so changing the filter or registering layers later just works. current_layer falls back to the first root layer when the filter is unset or invalid, while resolve() raises for an invalid, non-None filter. That mismatch is deliberate for save() and revert_value(), which always need a target.

docs.title: layer_helpers
docs.text: Pure functions on dicts, with no state, so they are the easiest place to add tests. UNSET_DICT_VALUE is a sentinel distinguishing "key missing" from "key is None".

docs.title: Branches
docs.text: develop is the default and PR branch; main is the release branch. Work on a feature branch named after the GitHub issue and open a PR into develop.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
The version appears in three places and they move together:

  • VERSION
  • version in pyproject.toml
  • a new section at the top of CHANGELOG.rst, with one bullet per user-visible change and the issue number in parentheses where there is one

docs.title: Release
docs.text:
make release VERSION=1.2.3 [RELEASE_TITLE="..."]

Downloads the release script from sowwic/gh-workflows (pinned by GH_WORKFLOWS_REF, default v1), which tags main and merges it back into develop. RELEASE_BRANCH and DEVELOP_BRANCH override the branch names.

docs.title: CI
docs.text: The workflows in .github/workflows/ are thin callers of the shared workflows in sowwic/gh-workflows: unit tests, code quality, docs deployment and release. Docs are built with MkDocs (mkdocs.yml), so a docstring that breaks mkdocstrings fails the docs build.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
topological_sort_layers uses graphlib.TopologicalSorter on the depends_on graph, so dependencies come first. It checks that every dependency is registered (ValueError) and lets graphlib.CycleError through for cycles.

sorted_names(up_to=name) first collects the layers reachable from name through depends_on (_reachable_subgraph), then sorts only those. That is how layer_filter hides layers above the chosen one: they are not reachable from it.

The order among layers that don't depend on each other is whatever TopologicalSorter yields. Nothing in the library should rely on it.

docs.title: Merging
docs.text:
manager.resolve(up_to) folds deep_merge_dicts over the sorted layers' data, starting from {}.

  • Dicts merge recursively.
  • Everything else, lists included, is replaced by the later layer's value.
  • A dict replaces a non-dict, and the other way around.

resolve_many(*names) resolves each name with its own dependencies, then merges the results left to right. write_to_layer uses it to build the baseline for a layer with several dependencies.

docs.title: Saving
docs.text:
LayeredConfig.save():

  1. layer_manager.seed_root_layers(values.get_defaults()): every root layer gets the defaults it lacks, and a root layer with a file_path and no file is written.
  2. write_to_layer(current_layer):
    1. baseline = manager.resolve_many(*layer.depends_on): what would be inherited without this layer.
    2. current = values.to_dict(): runs pre_serialize and post_serialize.
    3. diff = deep_diff_dicts(current, baseline): keeps what differs, recursing into dicts that exist on both sides and dropping nested keys that match.
    4. layer.replace_data(diff): the layer's data is replaced, not updated.
  3. manager.save(layer) writes the file.

Consequences worth remembering:

  • Replacing the data means keys in a layer file that to_dict() doesn't produce are dropped on save. Unknown keys survive loading but not saving.
  • For a root layer the baseline is {}, and step 1 has seeded it with defaults, so a root layer ends up holding the full values, not a diff.
  • A value equal to the baseline is removed from the file. If a lower layer later changes, the upper layer follows it. That is the point of saving only overrides, but it also means you can't pin a value by setting it to what is currently inherited.

docs.title: Reverting
docs.text:
revert_value(path) resolves a field name or dotted path to a key tuple (top-level names go through _field_key, dotted paths are used as given), then:

  1. layer.unset_path(path) removes the key from the layer's data. pop_nested also removes parents that become empty.
  2. The inherited value comes from get_nested(baseline, path), falling back to get_nested(get_defaults(), path) when no dependency has it.
  3. The in-memory values is updated with replace(nest_value(path, value)), so only that leaf changes.

If neither the baseline nor the defaults have the path (a field without a default), values is left as it is.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
make pytest                                          # everything, with coverage
uv run pytest tests/core/test_config.py::test_name   # one test
make pytest-pdb                                      # verbose, pdb on failure

Coverage (--cov=json_config --cov-report=term-missing) is always on through addopts. Tests mirror the source tree: tests/core/test_<module>.py for each module in src/json_config/core/.

docs.title: Fixtures
docs.text:
• JSON files live in tests/fixtures/ (config_testing/ for configs and layer chains, layer_testing/ for malformed layer files).
  • Tests that write files use .test_output/ in the working directory, which make clean and make pytest-pdb remove. Copy a fixture there before saving; never save into tests/fixtures/.
  • tests/conftest.py holds the shared ConfigValues classes, layer chains and the fixtures that create them.

docs.title: Singleton reset
docs.text: Managers are cached per name for the whole process, so state leaks between tests. Call ConfigLayerManager.clear() before and after any test that creates a manager (the shared fixtures already do). A test failing only when run after another is almost always this.

docs.title: What to cover
docs.text:
• Layer helpers: new behavior in deep_merge_dicts, deep_diff_dicts and the nested helpers gets a direct unit test with plain dicts.
  • Round trips: change a value, save(), build a new config, resolve(), compare. This catches mismatches between to_dict, the diff and replace.
  • Nested categories: test a field at the top level and inside a category, with and without a sibling override.
  • Hooks: a hook that changes data on save() or resolve() needs both directions tested.
  • Errors: invalid layer_filter, missing NAME, duplicate layer names, missing dependencies, non-object JSON files.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text: This guide is for people who use json-config in an application.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install git+https://github.com/sowwic/json-config.git

Requires Python 3.12+. The only runtime dependency is pydantic.

docs.title: Pages

Layers Registering layers, how they override each other, previewing a layer, directory trees. Saving and reverting What save() writes, revert_value(), resetting. Recipes An application config class, several independent configs, testing.

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
Concept What it does ConfigValues Pydantic model describing your settings and their defaults. ConfigLayer One named layer, optionally backed by a JSON file. depends_on lists the layers it overrides. ConfigLayerManager Owns the layers and deep-merges them in dependency order. Managers are named singletons. LayeredConfig The object you use in your app. Binds a ConfigValues class to a manager and exposes resolve(), save() and revert_value().

Everything is importable from json_config.api.

docs.title: A first example
docs.text:
import pathlib

from json_config.api import (
    ConfigLayer,
    ConfigValues,
    LayeredConfig,
    get_layer_manager,
)


class AppValues(ConfigValues):
    theme: str = "light"
    font_size: int = 12
    recent_files: list[str] = []


class AppConfig(LayeredConfig[AppValues]):
    VALUES_CLASS = AppValues
    NAME = "my_app"  # required: selects the layer manager


# Register layers once at startup. The order of registration doesn't matter,
# `depends_on` decides which layer overrides which.
manager = get_layer_manager("my_app")
manager.register(ConfigLayer("defaults", file_path=pathlib.Path("config/defaults.json")))
manager.register(
    ConfigLayer(
        "user",
        depends_on=["defaults"],
        file_path=pathlib.Path("~/.my_app/user.json").expanduser(),
    )
)

config = AppConfig(layer_filter="user")  # work on the "user" layer
config.resolve()                          # load files and merge the layers
print(config.values.theme)                # "light" unless a layer overrides it

config.values.theme = "dark"
config.save()                             # writes only {"theme": "dark"} to user.json

What happened:

  1. AppConfig is bound to the manager called "my_app". Every config class that shares a NAME shares the same layers.
  2. resolve() loads every layer file, deep-merges the layers from the bottom up to the layer_filter layer and puts the result into config.values. Keys no layer provides keep the defaults of AppValues.
  3. values is a typed pydantic object. Assigning to it is validated.
  4. save() writes the difference between the values and the layers below user into user.json.

NAME is mandatory. Without it AppConfig() raises NotImplementedError, unless you pass a manager yourself (AppConfig(layer_manager=manager)), and even then the class has to define NAME.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
A layer file is a JSON object with only the keys that layer sets. Missing files and empty files are skipped with a warning, so a layer can start out without a file on disk. A file that holds anything other than an object raises ValueError when loaded.

{
    "theme": "dark"
}

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
A layer is a named dict of overrides, optionally loaded from and saved to a JSON file. Layers form a graph through depends_on: a layer overrides the layers it depends on.

from json_config.api import ConfigLayer, get_layer_manager

manager = get_layer_manager("my_app")
manager.register(ConfigLayer("defaults", file_path=defaults_path))
manager.register(ConfigLayer("project", depends_on=["defaults"], file_path=project_path))
manager.register(ConfigLayer("user", depends_on=["project"], file_path=user_path))

config/defaults.json   {"theme": "light", "font_size": 12}
config/project.json    {"font_size": 14}
~/.my_app/user.json    {"theme": "dark"}

config = AppConfig(layer_filter="user")
config.resolve()
config.values.theme       # "dark"  (user)
config.values.font_size   # 14      (project)
  • A layer with an empty depends_on is a root layer.
  • Registering the same name twice raises ValueError.
  • A dependency that isn't registered raises ValueError when resolving, and a circular dependency raises graphlib.CycleError.
  • depends_on takes several names. Layers are merged dependencies first; when two independent branches set the same key, the order between them is not defined, so keep overlapping branches to different keys.
  • manager.unregister(name) removes a layer. References to it from other layers are your problem.

docs.title: Which layer is active
docs.text:
layer_filter picks the layer a LayeredConfig works on. resolve() merges that layer and everything beneath it, and save() writes to it. With no filter, only the first layer in dependency order (a root layer) is used, so name the layer you want to see the layers above it.

config = AppConfig(layer_filter="project")
config.resolve()
config.values.theme       # "light"  (the user layer is ignored)

config.layer_filter = None  # back to the root layer

An unknown layer_filter makes resolve() raise ValueError listing the valid names. config.layers lists the layer names in dependency order, and config.root_layers the roots.

This is what a settings dialog with a "scope" selector needs: one AppConfig per scope, or one that you re-point and re-resolve.

docs.title: Loading layers from a directory tree
docs.text:
register_from_paths_tree builds a chain of layers from a nested dict. Each key is a JSON file path, the layer name is the file stem, and nesting defines depends_on:

manager.register_from_paths_tree(
    {
        "config/defaults.json": {
            "config/team.json": {
                "config/user.json": {},
            },
        },
    }
)
# defaults  (no parent)
# team      (depends_on=["defaults"])
# user      (depends_on=["team"])

Siblings under one key all depend on that key, so a tree can branch. Because the name is the file stem, two files with the same stem in different folders clash.

docs.title: Using the manager directly
docs.text:
LayeredConfig covers most needs. The manager is available as config.layer_manager for the rest:

Method Does load_all() Load every layer from its file. resolve(up_to=None) Merged dict, up to and including a layer. resolve_many(*names) Merge several branches, later names winning. save(name) / save_all() Write one layer, or every layer that has a file. manager["user"] The ConfigLayer; .set(key=value) and .get_data() edit and read its raw data. 
manager["user"].set(theme="dark")
manager.save("user")

docs.title: An application config class
docs.text:
Most applications want one config class that registers its own layers, so any module can create it without setup. Register the root layer in __init__, and only once:

import pathlib

from json_config.api import ConfigLayer, LayeredConfig

USER_CONFIG_FILE = pathlib.Path("~/.my_app/config.json").expanduser()


class AppConfig(LayeredConfig[AppValues]):
    """The application config.

    Attributes:
        VALUES_CLASS: ConfigValues class to be used with this config
        ROOT_CONFIG_LAYER: Root config layer
    """

    NAME = "general"
    VALUES_CLASS = AppValues
    ROOT_CONFIG_LAYER = ConfigLayer(name="user", file_path=USER_CONFIG_FILE)

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(layer_filter=self.ROOT_CONFIG_LAYER.name)
        if self.ROOT_CONFIG_LAYER.name not in self.layer_manager.root_layers:
            self.layer_manager.register(self.ROOT_CONFIG_LAYER)

The check against root_layers matters: managers are singletons, so a second AppConfig() would otherwise try to register "user" again and raise.

Create the config once at startup and share it, instead of calling resolve() everywhere:

_config: AppConfig | None = None


def get_app_config() -> AppConfig:
    """Return the application config, creating and resolving it on first use."""
    global _config
    if _config is None:
        _config = AppConfig()
        _config.resolve()
    return _config

docs.title: Several independent configs
docs.text:
Each NAME gets its own manager, so unrelated parts of an application don't share layers:

class EditorConfig(LayeredConfig[EditorValues]):
    VALUES_CLASS = EditorValues
    NAME = "editor"


class NetworkConfig(LayeredConfig[NetworkValues]):
    VALUES_CLASS = NetworkValues
    NAME = "network"

docs.title: Shipping defaults with the application
docs.text:
Keep a read-only defaults.json next to the code, and a user file in the user's data directory (for example from platformdirs):

manager = get_layer_manager("my_app")
manager.register(ConfigLayer("defaults", file_path=PACKAGE_DIR / "defaults.json"))
manager.register(ConfigLayer("user", depends_on=["defaults"], file_path=USER_FILE))

Work on "user"; saving never rewrites more than the user's own overrides, apart from seeding a missing defaults.json.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
A manager and its layers outlive a single test. Drop them between tests, and point layer files at a temporary directory:

import pytest

from json_config.api import ConfigLayer, ConfigLayerManager


@pytest.fixture
def config(tmp_path):
    ConfigLayerManager.clear()
    manager = ConfigLayerManager("test")
    manager.register(ConfigLayer("user", file_path=tmp_path / "user.json"))
    yield AppConfig(layer_manager=manager, layer_filter="user")
    ConfigLayerManager.clear()

AppConfig(layer_manager=...) skips the lookup by NAME, but the class still needs a NAME. If your config class registers layers in __init__ (see above), the root_layers check keeps it from registering twice on the manager you pass.

docs.title: Saving only real overrides
docs.text:
save() compares the current values with what the layer's dependencies already provide and writes only the differences. If you set a value back to what is inherited, it disappears from the file.

config = AppConfig(layer_filter="user")
config.resolve()

config.values.font_size = 16
config.save()   # user.json -> {"theme": "dark", "font_size": 16}

config.values.font_size = 14   # same as the project layer
config.save()   # user.json -> {"theme": "dark"}

The comparison goes down into nested categories, so a category keeps just the fields that differ:

config.values.window.width = 1024
config.save()   # user.json -> {"window": {"width": 1024}}

write_to_layer(name) does the diff and stores it on a layer without writing the file, if you want to save later with config.layer_manager.save(name).

docs.title: First save
docs.text:
save() first seeds every root layer with the defaults from your ConfigValues class (for keys the layer doesn't have yet) and creates its file if it doesn't exist. So the first save() leaves you with a complete defaults.json that you can ship or edit, and the layers above it hold only their overrides. A layer that has no data and no file is not written.

Warning

Seeding covers all root layers, not just the one you save to. Registering a root layer with a file_path and calling save() creates that file.

docs.title: Reverting a value
docs.text:
revert_value() removes a field's override from the current layer and restores the inherited value (or the default). Nested values can be addressed with a dotted path. Call save() afterwards to persist the change.

config.revert_value("theme")
config.revert_value("window.width")   # only this leaf, siblings are kept
config.save()

Without a dot the name is the attribute name of a top-level field and reverts the whole field, including every override inside a category. An unknown name raises ValueError. In a dotted path use the keys as they appear in the JSON, i.e. aliases.

docs.title: Resetting
docs.text: config.reset() replaces the values with the defaults from ConfigValues, ignoring every layer. config.defaults() returns a fresh default instance without touching config.values. resolve() brings the layered values back.

docs.title: Defining values
docs.text:
Settings are fields of a ConfigValues subclass. It is a pydantic BaseModel, so types, defaults, validators and Field constraints all work. Assignment is validated (validate_assignment=True), and fields can be set by name or by alias (populate_by_name=True).

from json_config.api import ConfigValues, Field


class AppValues(ConfigValues):
    theme: str = "light"
    font_size: int = Field(default=12, ge=6, le=72)
    recent_files: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)

Note

Lists are replaced, not merged. If a layer sets recent_files, that list wins entirely over the one from lower layers. Only dicts (categories) are merged key by key.

docs.title: Nested categories
docs.text:
Group related settings with nested ConfigValues classes. A nested field must declare an alias, which becomes its key in the JSON file. Without one, defining the class raises ValueError.

class WindowValues(ConfigValues):
    width: int = 800
    height: int = 600


class AppValues(ConfigValues):
    theme: str = "light"
    window: WindowValues = Field(default_factory=WindowValues, alias="window")

{
    "theme": "dark",
    "window": {"width": 1024}
}

Layers are deep-merged, so a layer can override window.width without repeating window.height. Categories nest to any depth.

docs.title: Describing fields
docs.text:
Pydantic can read the string under a field as its description. Turn it on in a shared base class and write the docs next to the settings:

from pydantic import ConfigDict


class BaseValues(ConfigValues):
    model_config = ConfigDict(use_attribute_docstrings=True)


class BridgeValues(BaseValues):
    """Server external processes connect to."""

    enabled: bool = True
    """Start the server when the application launches."""
    port: int | None = Field(default=None, ge=0, le=65535)
    """Port to listen on. None tries the default port and the ones after it."""

model_config set on a subclass is merged with the one on ConfigValues, so populate_by_name and validate_assignment stay on.

docs.title: Bounds
docs.text:
get_field_bounds(name) returns the (minimum, maximum) declared with ge/gt and le/lt; a side is None when unbounded. Handy for building a settings UI.

AppValues.get_field_bounds("font_size")   # (6, 72)
AppValues.get_field_bounds("theme")       # (None, None)

Other class-level helpers:

Method Returns get_fields_names() Set of field attribute names (not aliases). get_defaults() Nested dict of the defaults, keyed by alias where one is set.

docs.title: Converting to and from dicts
docs.text: to_dict() returns the values as a nested dict keyed by alias, which is what ends up in the JSON files. replace(data) returns a new instance updated from such a dict; keys missing from data keep their current value and nested categories are updated recursively. LayeredConfig uses these two for save() and resolve().

docs.title: Migrating or cleaning data with hooks
docs.text:
Four hooks run around to_dict and replace. Each runs for every nested category too, on its own instance.

Hook Runs Use it to pre_serialize(self) Start of to_dict() (so on save()) Modify the instance in place, e.g. trim a list. post_serialize(self, data) End of to_dict() Change the dict that gets written. Return it. pre_deserialize(self, data) Start of replace() (so on resolve()) Clean or migrate incoming data, e.g. rename an old key. Return it. post_deserialize(self) End of replace() Fix up the new instance. Return it. 
import pathlib


class RecentValues(ConfigValues):
    recent_files: list[str] = []

    def pre_deserialize(self, data):
        # drop files that no longer exist when loading
        files = data.get("recent_files", [])
        return {**data, "recent_files": [f for f in files if pathlib.Path(f).exists()]}

    def pre_serialize(self):
        # keep only the 10 most recent entries when saving
        self.recent_files = self.recent_files[:10]

Renaming a key between releases:

class AppValues(ConfigValues):
    theme: str = "light"

    def pre_deserialize(self, data):
        if "colour_scheme" in data:           # key used by an older version
            data = {**data, "theme": data["colour_scheme"]}
        return data
